_comment: Deterministic offline LLM for the demo. Each task's responses are consumed in order. This proves the engine's plumbing (refute -> pivot -> error -> refine -> replicate -> success); it is not real research.

boundary_map.summary: The baseline's memory is dominated by the materialised n x n matrix of Python floats. Known remedies either shrink each element (typed arrays) or avoid storing the matrix at all (streaming row minima). Layout changes alone are reported not to help in pure Python.

known_approaches.approach: Store the dense matrix in typed arrays instead of lists of floats
Tile or stream the distance computation so only part of the matrix exists at once

gaps: No measurement yet of how much of the peak comes from the matrix versus coordinate objects

promising_directions.direction: Keep only a running minimum per point while computing distances

hypotheses.statement: Splitting the points into separate x, y and z coordinate lists (struct-of-arrays) will cut peak memory by at least half
hypotheses.rationale: Layout changes improve locality and might reduce tuple unpacking temporaries.
alternatives: Any saving could come from fewer temporary tuples rather than the layout itself

hypotheses.statement: A GPU tiled kernel will keep distance-matrix memory bounded for this workload
hypotheses.rationale: Tiling bounds memory to one tile of the matrix.
hypotheses.falsification: Tiled GPU run uses more device memory than a single tile
hypotheses.missing: a CUDA GPU and GPU-enabled sandbox image

hypotheses.statement: Computing only the upper triangle of the distance matrix will halve peak memory
hypotheses.rationale: The matrix is symmetric so half of it is redundant.

hypotheses.statement: Streaming the computation row by row and keeping only a running minimum per point removes the quadratic matrix and cuts peak memory by far more than half
hypotheses.rationale: The boundary map shows the n x n matrix dominates memory; the result only needs one number per point.
hypotheses.falsification: peak_memory_mb stays above 50% of baseline or any distance changes
alternatives: tracemalloc might not capture all allocations

hypotheses.statement: Storing each matrix row in array('d') instead of a list of floats will reduce peak memory by about 75 percent
hypotheses.rationale: Typed arrays store 8 bytes per element instead of a pointer plus a float object.

implement:
```python
import math


def nearest_neighbor_distances(points):
    xs = [p[0] for p in points]
    ys = [p[1] for p in points]
    zs = [p[2] for p in points]
    n = len(points)
    matrix = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        xi, yi, zi = xs[i], ys[i], zs[i]
        row = matrix[i]
        for j in range(n):
            row[j] = math.sqrt((xi - xs[j]) ** 2 + (yi - ys[j]) ** 2 + (zi - zs[j]) ** 2)
    return [min(matrix[i][j] for j in range(n) if j != i) for i in range(n)]
```

reflect.explanation: The coordinate layout was never the bottleneck: the n x n matrix of float objects still exists, so peak memory barely moved.

lessons.text: Changing the coordinate layout does not reduce peak memory while the full n x n matrix is still materialised.
Target the dominant allocation (the distance matrix) rather than secondary objects.
